entries.meaning: The women delight in the prospect of repeated hospitality for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa at their in-laws’ home. A friend observes that the two princes beside Daśaratha resemble the dark and fair pair: Bharata is so like Rāma that men and women cannot distinguish them at a glance, while Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna are alike from nail to crown. All four captivate the mind; their beauty cannot be spoken and has no comparison in the three worlds.

Thus everyone fulfils wishes in imagination and lets surging joy fill the heart. Even the kings who had attended Sītā’s self-choice rejoice on seeing all four brothers, praise Rāma’s vast stainless fame, and return to their lodgings. After some happy days the wedding date arrives in the lovely winter month of Agrahāyaṇa. The Creator weighs planet, lunar date, constellation, conjunction and weekday; Nārada sends the chosen hour, which Janaka’s astrologers confirm, and the Brahmins announce the pure cow-dust twilight as the root of every auspiciousness.

Janaka tells his family priest there is no reason to delay. Śatānanda summons ministers, assembles every auspicious object, and sets out with conches, drums, vessels, married women’s songs and Brahmins’ Vedic chants to fetch the wedding party. Before Daśaratha’s majesty even Indra seems insignificant. When the hosts announce that the hour has come, drums are struck; after consulting his guru and completing family rites, the king advances with sages and holy men, while Brahmā and the gods marvel at his fortune and deem their own births fruitless by comparison.

The gods recognize the auspicious hour, shower flowers and sound drums. Śiva, Brahmā and hosts of divinities mount many aerial cars, their bodies thrilled and hearts eager to witness Rāma’s wedding. Enchanted by Janakpur, they find their own worlds small and stare at its supernatural pavilions and its handsome, righteous and discerning people. Their own beauty seems like starlight before the moon. Even Brahmā is amazed to find no trace of his workmanship, until Śiva cautions them to remember calmly whose wedding this is—Sītā’s and Raghubīra’s.

Śiva reminds the gods that merely taking the couple’s names destroys every root of misfortune and places the four human aims in one’s palm: these are Sītā and Rāma. The heavenly party moves on and sees Daśaratha surrounded by holy men like holiness embodied, with his four sons shining beside him like liberation’s four forms. The dark-and-gold pairs kindle the gods’ love; when they behold Rāma they praise the king and rain flowers. Śiva and Umā gaze upon Rāma from nail to crown again and again, bodies thrilled and eyes wet.

Rāma’s dark body gleams like a peacock’s neck and his colourful garments put lightning to shame. Every wedding ornament upon him is auspicious; his autumn-moon face and fresh lotus eyes surpass comparison. His lovely brothers ride beside him, making their spirited horses dance while princes display fine mounts and genealogists chant family praise. The horse Rāma rides moves so splendidly that Garuḍa is abashed; steed and trappings seem as though Love himself fashioned them.

Not even Sarasvatī can describe the superb horse bearing Rāma. Absorbed in Rāma’s beauty, Śiva treasures all fifteen of his visible eyes; Viṣṇu too is enchanted together with Lakṣmī, and Brahmā rejoices yet regrets having only eight eyes. Skanda exults that his eyes yield one-and-a-half times Brahmā’s gain, while wise Indra considers Gautama’s curse—which covered him with eyes—a supreme blessing. All gods envy the thousand-eyed king of heaven, and both heavenly and royal assemblies rejoice in beholding Rāma.

Moon-faced, fawn-eyed women wear fine garments of many colours and every ornament; each one’s beauty humbles the pride of Love’s consort. With auspicious adornment they sing so sweetly that cuckoos seem ashamed, and bangles, girdles and anklets ring as their gait puts Love’s elephant to shame. Music and auspicious cries fill sky and city. Śacī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Bhavānī and other wise goddesses assume the finest women’s dress, enter the women’s palace unrecognized, and join the joyful wedding songs.

The queens restrain tears because the moment is auspicious and joyfully perform the groom’s welcoming rite. They carefully observe both Vedic prescription and family custom amid fivefold music, songs and layered cloth pathways. After offering lamps and arghya, they lead Rāma to the pavilion. Daśaratha and his company sit in such splendour that the guardians of the worlds are humbled; gods shower flowers, Brahmins chant benedictions, and the roar of heaven and city drowns out every separate sound. Rāma receives arghya and takes his seat.

Janaka and Daśaratha meet with deep affection and observe every Vedic and social courtesy. The two great kings shine together beyond any simile a poet can find; at last the poet can only compare each equal father-in-law to the other. Delighted gods shower flowers and sing their praise, declaring that since Brahmā created the world they have seen and heard of many weddings, but never before a ceremony, retinue, and pair of equal fathers so perfectly matched. Unearthly love spreads on both sides as Janaka respectfully leads Daśaratha into the pavilion.
